source: As Queequeg’s Ramadan, or Fasting and Humiliation, was to continue all day, I did not choose to disturb him till towards night-fall; for I cherish the greatest respect towards everybody’s religious obligations, never mind how comical, and could not find it in my heart to undervalue even a congregation of ants worshipping a toad-stool; or those other creatures in certain parts of our earth, who with a degree of footmanism quite unprecedented in other planets, bow down before the torso of a deceased landed proprietor merely on account of the inordinate possessions yet owned and rented in his name.

I say, we good Presbyterian Christians should be charitable in these things, and not fancy ourselves so vastly superior to other mortals, pagans and what not, because of their half-crazy conceits on these subjects. There was Queequeg, now, certainly entertaining the most absurd notions about Yojo and his Ramadan;—but what of that? Queequeg thought he knew what he was about, I suppose; he seemed to be content; and there let him rest. All our arguing with him would not avail; let him be, I say: and Heaven have mercy on us all—Presbyterians and Pagans alike—for we are all somehow dreadfully cracked about the head, and sadly need mending.

Towards evening, when I felt assured that all his performances and rituals must be over, I went up to his room and knocked at the door; but no answer. I tried to open it, but it was fastened inside. “Queequeg,” said I softly through the key-hole:—all silent. “I say, Queequeg! why don’t you speak? It’s I—Ishmael.” But all remained still as before. I began to grow alarmed. I had allowed him such abundant time; I thought he might have had an apoplectic fit. I looked through the key-hole; but the door opening into an odd corner of the room, the key-hole prospect was but a crooked and sinister one. I could only see part of the foot-board of the bed and a line of the wall, but nothing more. I was surprised to behold resting against the wall the wooden shaft of Queequeg’s harpoon, which the landlady the evening previous had taken from him, before our mounting to the chamber. That’s strange, thought I; but at any rate, since the harpoon stands yonder, and he seldom or never goes abroad without it, therefore he must be inside here, and no possible mistake.

“Queequeg!—Queequeg!”—all still. Something must have happened. Apoplexy! I tried to burst open the door; but it stubbornly resisted. Running down stairs, I quickly stated my suspicions to the first person I met—the chamber-maid. “La! la!” she cried, “I thought something must be the matter. I went to make the bed after breakfast, and the door was locked; and not a mouse to be heard; and it’s been just so silent ever since. But I thought, may be, you had both gone off and locked your baggage in for safe keeping. La! la, ma’am!—Mistress! murder! Mrs. Hussey! apoplexy!”—and with these cries, she ran towards the kitchen, I following.

Mrs. Hussey soon appeared, with a mustard-pot in one hand and a vinegar-cruet in the other, having just broken away from the occupation of attending to the castors, and scolding her little black boy meantime.

“Wood-house!” cried I, “which way to it? Run for God’s sake, and fetch something to pry open the door—the axe!—the axe! he’s had a stroke; depend upon it!”—and so saying I was unmethodically rushing up stairs again empty-handed, when Mrs. Hussey interposed the mustard-pot and vinegar-cruet, and the entire castor of her countenance.
“What’s the matter with you, young man?”
“Get the axe! For God’s sake, run for the doctor, some one, while I pry it open!”

“Look here,” said the landlady, quickly putting down the vinegar-cruet, so as to have one hand free; “look here; are you talking about prying open any of my doors?”—and with that she seized my arm. “What’s the matter with you? What’s the matter with you, shipmate?”

In as calm, but rapid a manner as possible, I gave her to understand the whole case. Unconsciously clapping the vinegar-cruet to one side of her nose, she ruminated for an instant; then exclaimed—“No! I haven’t seen it since I put it there.” Running to a little closet under the landing of the stairs, she glanced in, and returning, told me that Queequeg’s harpoon was missing. “He’s killed himself,” she cried. “It’s unfort’nate Stiggs done over again—there goes another counterpane—God pity his poor mother!—it will be the ruin of my house. Has the poor lad a sister? Where’s that girl?—there, Betty, go to Snarles the Painter, and tell him to paint me a sign, with—“no suicides permitted here, and no smoking in the parlor;”—might as well kill both birds at once. Kill? The Lord be merciful to his ghost! What’s that noise there? You, young man, avast there!”
And running up after me, she caught me as I was again trying to force open the door.

“I don’t allow it; I won’t have my premises spoiled. Go for the locksmith, there’s one about a mile from here. But avast!” putting her hand in her side-pocket, “here’s a key that’ll fit, I guess; let’s see.” And with that, she turned it in the lock; but, alas! Queequeg’s supplemental bolt remained unwithdrawn within.

“Have to burst it open,” said I, and was running down the entry a little, for a good start, when the landlady caught at me, again vowing I should not break down her premises; but I tore from her, and with a sudden bodily rush dashed myself full against the mark.

With a prodigious noise the door flew open, and the knob slamming against the wall, sent the plaster to the ceiling; and there, good heavens! there sat Queequeg, altogether cool and self-collected; right in the middle of the room; squatting on his hams, and holding Yojo on top of his head. He looked neither one way nor the other way, but sat like a carved image with scarce a sign of active life.
“Queequeg,” said I, going up to him, “Queequeg, what’s the matter with you?”
“He hain’t been a sittin’ so all day, has he?” said the landlady.

But all we said, not a word could we drag out of him; I almost felt like pushing him over, so as to change his position, for it was almost intolerable, it seemed so painfully and unnaturally constrained; especially, as in all probability he had been sitting so for upwards of eight or ten hours, going too without his regular meals.
“Mrs. Hussey,” said I, “he’s alive at all events; so leave us, if you please, and I will see to this strange affair myself.”

Closing the door upon the landlady, I endeavored to prevail upon Queequeg to take a chair; but in vain. There he sat; and all he could do—for all my polite arts and blandishments—he would not move a peg, nor say a single word, nor even look at me, nor notice my presence in the slightest way.

I wonder, thought I, if this can possibly be a part of his Ramadan; do they fast on their hams that way in his native island. It must be so; yes, it’s part of his creed, I suppose; well, then, let him rest; he’ll get up sooner or later, no doubt. It can’t last for ever, thank God, and his Ramadan only comes once a year; and I don’t believe it’s very punctual then.

I went down to supper. After sitting a long time listening to the long stories of some sailors who had just come from a plum-pudding voyage, as they called it (that is, a short whaling-voyage in a schooner or brig, confined to the north of the line, in the Atlantic Ocean only); after listening to these plum-puddingers till nearly eleven o’clock, I went up stairs to go to bed, feeling quite sure by this time Queequeg must certainly have brought his Ramadan to a termination. But no; there he was just where I had left him; he had not stirred an inch. I began to grow vexed with him; it seemed so downright senseless and insane to be sitting there all day and half the night on his hams in a cold room, holding a piece of wood on his head.
“For heaven’s sake, Queequeg, get up and shake yourself; get up and have some supper. You’ll starve; you’ll kill yourself, Queequeg.” But not a word did he reply.

Despairing of him, therefore, I determined to go to bed and to sleep; and no doubt, before a great while, he would follow me. But previous to turning in, I took my heavy bearskin jacket, and threw it over him, as it promised to be a very cold night; and he had nothing but his ordinary round jacket on. For some time, do all I would, I could not get into the faintest doze. I had blown out the candle; and the mere thought of Queequeg—not four feet off—sitting there in that uneasy position, stark alone in the cold and dark; this made me really wretched. Think of it; sleeping all night in the same room with a wide awake pagan on his hams in this dreary, unaccountable Ramadan!

But somehow I dropped off at last, and knew nothing more till break of day; when, looking over the bedside, there squatted Queequeg, as if he had been screwed down to the floor. But as soon as the first glimpse of sun entered the window, up he got, with stiff and grating joints, but with a cheerful look; limped towards me where I lay; pressed his forehead again against mine; and said his Ramadan was over.

Now, as I before hinted, I have no objection to any person’s religion, be it what it may, so long as that person does not kill or insult any other person, because that other person don’t believe it also. But when a man’s religion becomes really frantic; when it is a positive torment to him; and, in fine, makes this earth of ours an uncomfortable inn to lodge in; then I think it high time to take that individual aside and argue the point with him.

And just so I now did with Queequeg. “Queequeg,” said I, “get into bed now, and lie and listen to me.” I then went on, beginning with the rise and progress of the primitive religions, and coming down to the various religions of the present time, during which time I labored to show Queequeg that all these Lents, Ramadans, and prolonged ham-squattings in cold, cheerless rooms were stark nonsense; bad for the health; useless for the soul; opposed, in short, to the obvious laws of Hygiene and common sense. I told him, too, that he being in other things such an extremely sensible and sagacious savage, it pained me, very badly pained me, to see him now so deplorably foolish about this ridiculous Ramadan of his. Besides, argued I, fasting makes the body cave in; hence the spirit caves in; and all thoughts born of a fast must necessarily be half-starved. This is the reason why most dyspeptic religionists cherish such melancholy notions about their hereafters. In one word, Queequeg, said I, rather digressively; hell is an idea first born on an undigested apple-dumpling; and since then perpetuated through the hereditary dyspepsias nurtured by Ramadans.

I then asked Queequeg whether he himself was ever troubled with dyspepsia; expressing the idea very plainly, so that he could take it in. He said no; only upon one memorable occasion. It was after a great feast given by his father the king, on the gaining of a great battle wherein fifty of the enemy had been killed by about two o’clock in the afternoon, and all cooked and eaten that very evening.

“No more, Queequeg,” said I, shuddering; “that will do;” for I knew the inferences without his further hinting them. I had seen a sailor who had visited that very island, and he told me that it was the custom, when a great battle had been gained there, to barbecue all the slain in the yard or garden of the victor; and then, one by one, they were placed in great wooden trenchers, and garnished round like a pilau, with breadfruit and cocoanuts; and with some parsley in their mouths, were sent round with the victor’s compliments to all his friends, just as though these presents were so many Christmas turkeys.

After all, I do not think that my remarks about religion made much impression upon Queequeg. Because, in the first place, he somehow seemed dull of hearing on that important subject, unless considered from his own point of view; and, in the second place, he did not more than one third understand me, couch my ideas simply as I would; and, finally, he no doubt thought he knew a good deal more about the true religion than I did. He looked at me with a sort of condescending concern and compassion, as though he thought it a great pity that such a sensible young man should be so hopelessly lost to evangelical pagan piety.

At last we rose and dressed; and Queequeg, taking a prodigiously hearty breakfast of chowders of all sorts, so that the landlady should not make much profit by reason of his Ramadan, we sallied out to board the Pequod, sauntering along, and picking our teeth with halibut bones.

I almost felt like pushing him over just to change his position, which was almost unbearable to look at — so painfully and unnaturally stiff. Especially since, in all likelihood, he had been sitting that way for upwards of eight or ten hours, going without his regular meals the whole time.
"Mrs. Hussey," said I, "he's alive, at any rate. So leave us, please, and I'll deal with this strange business myself."

Closing the door on the landlady, I tried to get Queequeg to sit in a chair, but it was useless. There he sat. Despite all my polite efforts and coaxing, he wouldn't budge an inch, say a single word, look at me, or show the slightest awareness that I was there.

I wonder, I thought, if this could be part of his Ramadan. Do they fast while squatting like this on his native island? It must be so. Yes, it's part of his religion, I suppose. Well, let him be. He'll get up sooner or later. It can't last forever, thank God. And his Ramadan only comes once a year — and I don't think it's very punctual even then.

I went down to supper. After sitting a long time listening to the rambling stories of some sailors who had just come from a "plum-pudding voyage," as they called it — meaning a short whaling trip in a schooner or brig, limited to waters north of the equator in the Atlantic Ocean — after listening to these plum-puddingers until nearly eleven o'clock, I went upstairs to bed, feeling quite sure by then that Queequeg must have finished his Ramadan. But no — there he was, exactly where I had left him. He hadn't moved an inch. I started getting annoyed with him. It seemed so utterly senseless and insane to sit there all day and half the night on his heels in a cold room, holding a piece of wood on his head.
"For heaven's sake, Queequeg, get up and move around. Get up and have some supper. You'll starve. You'll kill yourself, Queequeg." But not a word did he reply.

Giving up on him, I decided to go to bed and sleep. No doubt he would follow before long. But before turning in, I took my heavy bearskin jacket and threw it over him, since it promised to be a very cold night and he had nothing but his ordinary short sailor's jacket on. For some time, no matter what I did, I couldn't fall asleep. I had blown out the candle, and the mere thought of Queequeg — not four feet away — sitting in that miserable position, completely alone in the cold and dark — it made me truly wretched. Think of it: sleeping all night in the same room with a wide-awake pagan squatting in this dreary, inexplicable Ramadan!

But somehow I drifted off at last and knew nothing more until daybreak. Looking over the side of the bed, there squatted Queequeg, as if he had been bolted to the floor. But as soon as the first rays of sun entered the window, up he got, with stiff and creaking joints but a cheerful face. He limped over to where I lay, pressed his forehead against mine again, and said his Ramadan was over.

Now, as I mentioned before, I have no objection to anyone's religion, whatever it may be, as long as that person doesn't kill or insult anyone else for not sharing it. But when a person's religion becomes truly fanatical — when it's a source of real torment, and when, in short, it makes this earth of ours an uncomfortable place to live — then I think it's high time to take that individual aside and have a serious talk.

And that's exactly what I did with Queequeg. "Queequeg," I said, "get into bed and lie down and listen to me." I then launched into a review, beginning with the rise and development of primitive religions and working my way down to the various religions of today. Throughout, I tried to show Queequeg that all these Lents, Ramadans, and long hours of squatting in cold, cheerless rooms were complete nonsense — bad for the health, useless for the soul, and contrary to the basic laws of hygiene and common sense. I told him that since he was in other respects such an extremely sensible and shrewd savage, it pained me — deeply pained me — to see him being so foolish about this ridiculous Ramadan of his. Besides, I argued, fasting weakens the body, which weakens the spirit, and all thoughts born of fasting are necessarily half-starved. This is the reason why most dyspeptic religious people — those with chronic indigestion — cherish such gloomy notions about their hereafters. In a word, Queequeg, I said, getting somewhat off track: hell is an idea first born from an undigested apple dumpling, and has been perpetuated ever since through the hereditary indigestion caused by Ramadans.

I then asked Queequeg whether he himself was ever troubled with indigestion, putting the question very plainly so he could understand. He said no — except on one memorable occasion. It was after a great feast given by his father, the king, celebrating a great battle in which fifty of the enemy had been killed by about two in the afternoon and all cooked and eaten that very evening.

"No more, Queequeg," I said, shuddering. "That will do." I knew what he was implying without him spelling it out. I had met a sailor who had visited that very island, and he told me that when a great battle was won there, the custom was to barbecue all the slain in the victor's yard or garden. Then, one by one, they were placed on great wooden platters, garnished around like a pilaf with breadfruit and coconuts, and with parsley in their mouths, were sent round with the victor's compliments to all his friends — just as though these gifts were so many Christmas turkeys.

In the end, I don't think my remarks about religion made much of an impression on Queequeg. In the first place, he seemed somewhat deaf to that particular subject, unless it was approached from his own point of view. In the second place, he didn't understand more than a third of what I said, no matter how simply I put it. And finally, he no doubt believed he knew a good deal more about true religion than I did. He looked at me with a sort of condescending pity and compassion, as though he thought it a great shame that such a sensible young man should be so hopelessly lost to evangelical pagan piety.

At last we got up and dressed. Queequeg ate a tremendously hearty breakfast of chowders of every kind, making sure the landlady wouldn't profit too much from his Ramadan. Then we headed out to board the Pequod, strolling along and picking our teeth with halibut bones.

modern_da.title: Kapitel 17 — Ramadanen
paragraphs: Da Queequegs ramadan, eller faste og ydmygelse, skulle vare hele dagen, valgte jeg ikke at forstyrre ham før hen mod aften. For jeg har den største respekt for alles religiøse pligter, uanset hvor komiske de er, og jeg kunne ikke få mig selv til at se ned på så meget som en forsamling af myrer, der tilbeder en fluesvamp — eller på de andre væsner i visse dele af vores jord, som med en lakajagtig underdanighed, der er ukendt på andre planeter, bukker sig for torsoen af en afdød godsejer alene på grund af de enorme ejendomme, der stadig ejes og udlejes i hans navn.

Jeg siger, vi gode presbyterianske kristne bør være overbærende med den slags. Vi skal ikke anse os selv for så uendeligt overlegne i forhold til andre mennesker — hedninge og hvem det nu er — på grund af deres halvgale idéer om disse emner. Der var Queequeg, som bestemt havde de mest absurde forestillinger om Yojo og hans ramadan — men hvad så? Queequeg troede vel, han vidste, hvad han gjorde. Han virkede tilfreds, og dér burde jeg lade ham være. Al vores diskussion med ham ville ikke hjælpe. Lad ham være, siger jeg, og himlen være os alle nådig — både presbyterianere og hedninge — for vi er alle på en eller anden måde forfærdeligt skøre i hovedet og trænger slemt til at blive lappet sammen.

Hen mod aften, da jeg var sikker på, at alle hans ritualer måtte være slut, gik jeg op til hans værelse og bankede på døren. Intet svar. Jeg prøvede at åbne den, men den var låst indefra. »Queequeg,« sagde jeg sagte gennem nøglehullet. Alt var stille. »Hør nu, Queequeg! Hvorfor svarer du ikke? Det er mig — Ishmael.« Men alt forblev lige så stille som før. Jeg begyndte at blive bekymret. Jeg havde givet ham rigeligt med tid. Jeg tænkte, at han kunne have fået et slagtilfælde. Jeg kiggede gennem nøglehullet, men da døren åbnede sig mod et underligt hjørne af værelset, var udsigten gennem nøglehullet kun skæv og uhyggelig. Jeg kunne kun se en del af sengens fodende og en strimmel væg, ikke andet. Jeg blev overrasket over at se træskaftet på Queequegs harpun stå lænet op ad væggen — værtinden havde taget den fra ham aftenen før, inden vi gik op på værelset. Det er mærkeligt, tænkte jeg. Men da harpunen var der, og han næsten aldrig gik nogen steder uden den, måtte han være derinde. Ingen tvivl om det.

»Queequeg! — Queequeg!« — stadig intet. Der måtte være sket noget. Et slagtilfælde! Jeg prøvede at tvinge døren op, men den holdt fast. Jeg løb ned ad trappen og forklarede hurtigt min frygt for den første, jeg mødte — stuepigen. »Du godeste!« råbte hun. »Jeg tænkte nok, der var noget galt. Jeg gik for at rede sengen efter morgenmaden, og døren var låst. Ikke en musestille lyd, og det har været lige så stille lige siden. Men jeg troede, I måske begge to var gået ud og havde låst jeres ting inde for at have dem i sikkerhed. Du godeste, frue! — Madam! Mord! Mrs. Hussey! Et slagtilfælde!« Og med de råb løb hun mod køkkenet, og jeg lige i hælene på hende.

Mrs. Hussey kom snart til syne med en sennepskrukke i den ene hånd og en eddikeflaske i den anden, netop afbrudt i at passe sine bordstativer (stativerne, der holder bordets krydderiflasker) og i at skælde ud på sin lille sorte dreng på samme tid.

»Brændeskuret!« råbte jeg. »Hvilken vej er det? Løb, for Guds skyld, og hent noget til at bryde døren op — øksen! Øksen! Han har fået et slagtilfælde, det er jeg sikker på!« Og mens jeg sagde det, var jeg på vej op ad trappen igen i fuldstændig uorden og tomhændet, da Mrs. Hussey spærrede vejen for mig med sennepskrukken, eddikeflasken og hele krydderistativet i sit ansigt.
»Hvad er der i vejen med dig, unge mand?«
»Hent øksen! For Guds skyld, løb nogen efter lægen, mens jeg bryder den op!«

»Hør her,« sagde værtinden og satte hurtigt eddikeflasken fra sig for at få en hånd fri. »Hør her — taler du om at bryde en af mine døre op?« Og med det greb hun fat i min arm. »Hvad er der i vejen med dig? Hvad er der i vejen med dig, skibsmakker?«

Så roligt og hurtigt som jeg kunne forklarede jeg situationen. Uden at tænke over det pressede hun eddikeflasken mod den ene side af sin næse, tænkte et øjeblik og udbrød så: »Nej! Jeg har ikke set den, siden jeg stillede den derhen.« Hun løb hen til et lille skab under trappen, kiggede ind, kom tilbage og fortalte mig, at Queequegs harpun var væk. »Han har slået sig selv ihjel,« råbte hun. »Det er stakkels Stiggs om igen — der går endnu et sengetæppe — Gud trøste hans stakkels mor! Det bliver mit hus' ruin. Har den stakkels dreng en søster? Hvor er den pige? — her, Betty, gå hen til Snarles maleren og sig, han skal male mig et skilt: ›Selvmord forbudt her, og rygning forbudt i stuen.‹ Man kan lige så godt dræbe to fluer med ét smæk. Dræbe? Herren være hans ånd nådig! Hvad er det for en lyd deroppe? Du, unge mand, bliv stående!«
Og hun løb op efter mig og fik fat i mig, netop som jeg igen prøvede at tvinge døren op.

»Det tillader jeg ikke; jeg vil ikke have mit hus ødelagt. Hent låsesmeden — der er en cirka en engelsk mil herfra. Men vent!« og hun stak hånden i sin sidelomme, »her er en nøgle, der passer, tror jeg; lad os se.« Og med det drejede hun den i låsen; men, ak! Queequegs ekstra slå var skudt for indefra.

»Den må brydes op,« sagde jeg og løb tilbage ad gangen for at tage tilløb, da værtinden greb fat i mig igen og insisterede på, at jeg ikke skulle bryde hendes ejendom ned. Men jeg rev mig løs og kastede mig med et pludseligt stød med hele kroppen mod døren.

Med et vældigt brag fløj døren op, håndtaget smækkede ind i væggen og sendte puds op til loftet. Og dér — du gode himmel! — dér sad Queequeg, helt kold og rolig, midt på gulvet, sidende på hælene med Yojo oven på hovedet. Han så hverken til den ene eller den anden side, men sad som en udskåret statue med knap et tegn på liv.
»Queequeg,« sagde jeg og gik hen til ham, »Queequeg, hvad er der i vejen med dig?«
»Han har da ikke siddet sådan hele dagen, vel?« sagde værtinden.

Men uanset hvad vi sagde, kunne vi ikke få et eneste ord ud af ham. Jeg var lige ved at skubbe ham omkuld, bare for at han kunne komme ud af den stilling, som var næsten ulidelig at se på — så smerteligt og unaturligt stiv. Især fordi han højst sandsynligt havde siddet sådan i mere end otte eller ti timer og så længe havde været uden sine almindelige måltider.
»Mrs. Hussey,« sagde jeg, »han lever i hvert fald. Så lad os være alene, tak, så skal jeg selv klare den her mærkelige sag.«

Jeg lukkede døren efter værtinden og prøvede at få Queequeg til at sætte sig på en stol, men det var ingen nytte til. Der sad han. Trods alle mine høflige forsøg og overtalelser rørte han sig ikke en tomme, sagde ikke et ord, så ikke på mig og viste ikke det mindste tegn på, at han vidste, at jeg var der.

Jeg undrer mig, tænkte jeg, om det her mon kan være en del af hans ramadan. Faster de, mens de sidder på hug sådan, på hans hjemø? Det må være sådan. Ja, det hører vist med til hans religion. Nå, lad ham være. Han rejser sig før eller siden. Det kan ikke vare evigt, Gud ske lov. Og hans ramadan kommer jo kun én gang om året — og jeg tror ikke engang, den er særlig punktlig.

Jeg gik ned og spiste aftensmad. Jeg blev længe siddende og lyttede til de vidtløftige historier fra nogle sømænd, som netop var kommet hjem fra en »plumbudding-rejse,« som de kaldte det — det vil sige en kort hvalfangertur i en skonnert eller brig, begrænset til farvandene nord for ækvator i Atlanterhavet. Efter at have lyttet til disse plumbuddinger til næsten klokken elleve gik jeg op for at sove og var nu ret sikker på, at Queequeg måtte have fuldført sin ramadan. Men nej — der var han, nøjagtig hvor jeg havde forladt ham. Han havde ikke rørt sig en tomme. Jeg begyndte at blive gal på ham. Det virkede så fuldstændig meningsløst og vanvittigt at sidde der hele dagen og halvdelen af natten på hælene i et koldt værelse med et stykke træ på hovedet.
»For himlens skyld, Queequeg, rejs dig og bevæg dig lidt. Rejs dig og få noget aftensmad. Du sulter ihjel. Du slår dig selv ihjel, Queequeg.« Men et ord svarede han ikke.

Jeg opgav ham og besluttede at gå i seng og sove. Han ville uden tvivl komme efter før længe. Men inden jeg lagde mig, tog jeg min tykke bjørnskindsjakke og kastede den over ham, for det lovede at blive en meget kold nat, og han havde ikke andet på end sin almindelige korte sømandsjakke. I nogen tid kunne jeg ikke falde i søvn, uanset hvad jeg gjorde. Jeg havde pustet lyset ud, og blot tanken om Queequeg — ikke fire fod fra mig — siddende i den elendige stilling, helt alene i kulde og mørke — den gjorde mig virkelig ulykkelig. Tænk bare: at sove hele natten i samme værelse som en lysvågen hedning, der sidder på hug i denne trøstesløse, uforklarlige ramadan!

Men på en eller anden måde gled jeg endelig ind i søvnen og vidste ikke af noget mere før daggry. Da jeg så ud over sengekanten, sad Queequeg der på hug, som om han var boltet fast til gulvet. Men så snart de første solstråler faldt ind ad vinduet, rejste han sig med stive, knirkende led, men med et gladt ansigt. Han humpede hen til der, hvor jeg lå, pressede panden mod min igen og sagde, at hans ramadan var forbi.

Nu har jeg, som jeg sagde før, ingen indvendinger mod noget menneskes religion, hvad den end er, så længe det menneske ikke dræber eller fornærmer andre, fordi de ikke deler den. Men når et menneskes religion bliver virkelig fanatisk — når den er en kilde til ægte pine, og når den kort sagt gør vores jord til et ubehageligt sted at bo — så synes jeg, at det er på høje tid at tage vedkommende til side og få en alvorlig samtale.

Og det var netop, hvad jeg gjorde med Queequeg. »Queequeg,« sagde jeg, »kom i seng og læg dig ned og hør på mig.« Så gik jeg i gang med en gennemgang, der begyndte med de primitive religioners opståen og udvikling og arbejdede sig ned til nutidens forskellige religioner. Hele vejen igennem forsøgte jeg at vise Queequeg, at alle de her fastetider, ramadaner og lange timer på hug i kolde, trøstesløse værelser var rent nonsens — dårligt for helbredet, ubrugeligt for sjælen og i strid med hygiejnens og den sunde fornufts grundlove. Jeg sagde til ham, at da han i alle andre henseender var en overordentlig fornuftig og skarp vilde, gjorde det mig ondt — dybt ondt — at se ham opføre sig så tåbeligt med denne latterlige ramadan. Desuden, hævdede jeg, svækker faste kroppen, og det svækker ånden, og alle tanker, der er født af faste, er nødvendigvis halvt udsultede. Det er grunden til, at de fleste dyspeptiske religiøse mennesker — dem med kronisk dårlig fordøjelse — nærer så dystre forestillinger om deres tilværelse efter døden. Kort sagt, Queequeg, sagde jeg, mens jeg kom lidt på afveje: Helvede er en idé, der først blev født af en ufordøjet æblekage og siden er blevet holdt i live gennem den arvelige dårlige fordøjelse, som ramadaner giver.

Så spurgte jeg Queequeg, om han selv nogensinde var plaget af dårlig fordøjelse, og stillede spørgsmålet helt enkelt, så han kunne forstå det. Han sagde nej — undtagen ved én mindeværdig lejlighed. Det var efter en stor fest, som hans far, kongen, holdt for at fejre en stor kamp, hvor halvtreds af fjenderne var blevet dræbt ved to-tiden om eftermiddagen og alle var blevet kogt og spist samme aften.

»Ikke mere, Queequeg,« sagde jeg og gyste. »Det er nok.« Jeg vidste, hvad han mente, uden at han behøvede at sige det ligeud. Jeg havde mødt en sømand, der havde besøgt netop den ø, og han havde fortalt mig, at når der var vundet en stor kamp dér, var skikken at grille alle de faldne i sejrherrens gård eller have. Så blev de ét for ét lagt på store trætallerkener, pyntet rundt om som en pilaf med brødfrugt og kokosnødder, og med persille i munden blev de sendt rundt med sejrherrens komplimenter til alle hans venner — ganske som var disse gaver lige så mange julekalkuner.

Alt i alt tror jeg ikke, at mine bemærkninger om religion gjorde det store indtryk på Queequeg. For det første virkede han lidt døv over for netop det emne, medmindre det blev grebet an fra hans eget synspunkt. For det andet forstod han ikke mere end en tredjedel af, hvad jeg sagde, uanset hvor enkelt jeg udtrykte mig. Og endelig troede han uden tvivl, at han vidste en hel del mere om sand religion end jeg. Han så på mig med en slags nedladende medlidenhed og medfølelse, som om han syntes, det var synd og skam, at sådan en fornuftig ung mand skulle være så håbløst fortabt for den evangeliske hedenske fromhed.

Til sidst stod vi op og klædte os på. Queequeg spiste en overvældende solid morgenmad med alle slags chowder og sørgede for, at værtinden ikke tjente for meget på hans ramadan. Så gik vi ud for at gå om bord på Pequod, mens vi pillede tænder med helleflynderknogler.
